opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most underrated questions in the field right now. A lot of people assume the state should just be the raw observation, the pixels or the tokens, and that if you have a big enough model it will figure out the rest. I don't think that's right.

For decision-making, a good state isn't a faithful copy of the world. It's a compression of the world that keeps what matters for acting and predicting, and throws away everything else. If you're crossing a street, you don't need to model the exact texture of every leaf on the trees. You need to know where the cars are, how fast they're moving, and roughly what they'll do next. So the state should be abstract, but in a grounded way, and it has to support prediction. If I take this action, what will the next state look like? That's where the world model idea comes in.

That's also why I'm a bit skeptical of approaches that do all the prediction in pixel space. Generating beautiful video frames is impressive, but it spends a huge amount of capacity on details that are irrelevant for decisions. I'd rather learn a latent space where the dynamics are simpler and more structured, where objects, spatial relationships, and causal factors are somehow disentangled, and then plan in that space.

Another point people sometimes miss is that the state shouldn't come only from language. Language is a wonderful interface, and it carries a lot of human knowledge, but it's a very lossy description of the physical world. A lot of what you need to act, like spatial layout, 3D structure, and continuity over time, is visual and embodied. So I believe vision, and more broadly sensory representation learning, has to be at the core of how we build these states, not just an add-on that gets translated into text.

And finally, I think the state has to be memory-aware. The real world is partially observable. What you see right now isn't enough. You need to integrate over time, remember what's behind you, keep track of things that went out of view. So a good state is less like a snapshot and more like a continuously updated belief about the world.

If I had to summarize, it should be compact, predictive, grounded in perception, and persistent over time. We're still quite far from having representations that really do all of those well, and I think that's one of the most exciting open problems.

r001.rationale: The response says a state should keep what matters for acting and predicting, and illustrates this with the information needed to cross a street.

r002.rationale: It describes abstract, structured latent states, but does not say representations are learned hierarchically or progressively built at increasing levels of abstraction.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because it sits right at the boundary between vision and action, and I come at it from the vision side.

My honest answer is that the state should not be a reconstruction of the environment. A lot of people's instinct is that if you want a model to make good decisions, you should first give it a complete picture, pixel by pixel, of what the world looks like, and then let a planner operate on that. I think that's the wrong target. Prediction in pixel space spends almost all of its capacity on things that don't matter for the decision. The exact texture of a wall, the way light flickers on water, the noise of a camera sensor. None of that changes what you should do next, but a generative model has to pay for all of it.

So the way I'd put it is: a good state is the smallest thing you can carry forward that still lets you predict the consequences of your actions. It's a compressed, predictive summary, not a photograph. And the compression should be learned, not hand-designed, because we are not good at guessing in advance which features will matter.

There's a second property I care about, which is that the representation should live in a space where "what happens next" is simple. If the dynamics in the latent space are smooth and roughly linear, then planning becomes tractable, and the model can look several steps ahead without errors blowing up. That's really the whole appeal of doing world modeling in representation space rather than in observation space. You are choosing a coordinate system where the future is easy to write down.

I'd also say the state has to be grounded in self-supervision from real sensory input. I don't think you get there by labeling. You get there by having the model predict masked or future parts of its own experience, in representation space, so that it's forced to abstract away the unpredictable noise and keep what is stable and causal. That's the lesson I take from the self-supervised learning work over the last few years, and I think it transfers directly to agents.

And then one more thing, which is almost a design philosophy. Good representations should be shared. The same state that lets you recognize an object should be the state that lets you reason about pushing it. We've spent too long training separate perception and control stacks and then gluing them together. If the representation is right, there isn't a seam there.

r001.rationale: The response says the state should retain only what is needed to predict the consequences of actions and discard details that do not matter for the decision, tying retained information to decision needs.

r002.rationale: The response discusses compression and abstraction, but does not describe hierarchical representation learning or progressively building more abstract representations.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what does the agent need to know to make a decision? A useful state representation doesn’t necessarily preserve every detail of the environment. It preserves the information that matters for predicting what could happen next and how the agent’s actions could affect it.

For example, a single image might tell you where an object is, but not whether it’s moving toward you or away from you. So the state may need to incorporate history, not just the current observation. And when the environment is only partially observable, it should represent uncertainty rather than pretend that everything is known.

So I would think of state as a compact, task-relevant summary of the agent’s experience—something that supports prediction and action. The challenge is deciding what you can safely discard without losing information that will matter for a future decision.

r001.rationale: It says a state should preserve information that matters for predicting outcomes and choosing actions, calling it a task-relevant summary.

r002.rationale: It does not describe hierarchical representation learning or progressively constructing more abstract representations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a useful state representation should preserve the information you need to decide what to do next. That doesn’t necessarily mean reconstructing every detail of the environment. It means capturing what matters for the task: what’s there, how things relate, and how they might change when you take an action.

And a single observation may not be enough. If you see an image of a ball, you don’t know which direction it’s moving. You need some history, or an internal representation that carries that information forward. In a partially observed environment, you also want to represent uncertainty about what you can’t see.

So I would judge the representation by whether it supports prediction and action: can it help you anticipate the consequences of different choices? A representation can be very good for recognizing objects and still miss something essential for making decisions.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a state should preserve information needed to decide what to do and capture what matters for the task.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses useful state information and history, but does not describe hierarchical representation learning or progressively more abstract representations.
